evals.prompt:
# We cannot demonstrate what "delete my account" actually did

## Problem Description

ACC-140 adds self-serve account deletion. Legal has already told us that when a
regulator or a customer asks us to demonstrate what deletion did, "the account
can no longer sign in" is not an answer we can give.

That is genuinely all our current test evidence shows. The old manual pass for
the admin-initiated version consists of deleting an account and confirming the
login page rejects it. Nobody has ever checked what happened anywhere else, and
the retention policy the deletion is supposed to honour has never been referred
to by a single test case.

Both documents are below: the story as product wrote it, and the retention
policy it has to comply with. They do not agree with each other everywhere.

## Output Specification

1. Produce `docs/test-cases/ACC-140.md` containing a single markdown table for
   the manual pass, plus any notes the reader needs.
2. The document has to be usable as evidence: someone reading a row must be
   able to see what was checked and against which written rule.
3. Out of scope: automated tests, the backup system's own restore procedure,
   and drafting the customer-facing privacy notice.
evals.expected_output:
1. Produce `docs/test-cases/ACC-140.md` containing a single markdown table for
   the manual pass, plus any notes the reader needs.
2. The document has to be usable as evidence: someone reading a row must be
   able to see what was checked and against which written rule.
3. Out of scope: automated tests, the backup system's own restore procedure,
   and drafting the customer-facing privacy notice.
assertions: docs/test-cases/ACC-140.md exists and contains a markdown table with rows. Scores zero if prose only or written elsewhere.

Rows assert consequences no screen shows: the privacy audit entry from R3 with its recorded fields, the sub-processor deletion instructions from R4, and the reassignment of workspace content from R5. Scores zero if every expected result in the table is a sign-in, screen or email observation. Covering only one of the three scores at most half.

Rows cover restoring by signing in inside the window, the last day on which restore still works, and the first day on which it does not, with the day counted explicitly in the precondition. Scores zero if the only grace-period row is 'the user can restore within 30 days'. One-sided coverage scores at most half.

The document states that AC-4's erasure cannot be complete while R2 keeps invoices with the legal name for 7 years and R1 keeps backups for 90 days, and either covers this as a case with the retained data as the expected result or raises it as a contradiction product has to resolve. Scores zero if erasure is asserted as total anywhere with no reference to the retained categories.

Every row names the specific AC bullet or policy clause it verifies - AC-3, R4 - because the document is evidence. A field carrying only 'story', 'policy', 'requirements' or nothing at all fails its purpose: three or more such rows score zero here, one or two score at most half.

A row covers deletion attempted by the sole owner of a workspace with other members, marked as blocked on the open product question rather than given an invented expected result. Scores zero if the path is absent; scores at most half if an outcome is asserted as though the story had decided it.

At least two rows cover attempts that must not proceed as normal - wrong password at confirmation, the confirmation word mistyped, an account with an unpaid balance or an open dispute, or a sign-in attempt after the erasure has completed. Scores zero if every row is a successful deletion.

Preconditions name the standing that changes the outcome - sole owner, member, has invoices, is inside or past the window - rather than a uniform 'a logged-in user'. Scores zero if no precondition field exists.

evals.prompt:
# Clinic booking rules keep failing exactly at their own limits

## Problem Description

BOOK-77 is the patient-facing slot booking for our clinic pilot. The rules are
all "no more than" and "no less than" style limits, and every defect we have
had on the previous version of this screen landed on or next to one of those
limits rather than in the middle of the allowed range: a slot exactly two hours
away that the API accepted and the UI hid, and a patient who ended up with four
upcoming appointments because a cancelled one was still being counted.

Reception is running acceptance on this manually. They want a list they can
work through in a session, and they want it to be obvious that the limits
themselves were exercised rather than a comfortable value in the middle of each
range.

The story below is what the backlog carries. Read the acceptance criteria and
the implementation note together; some of what a tester needs is only in the
note, and at least one thing a tester needs is in neither.

## Output Specification

1. Produce `docs/test-cases/BOOK-77.md` containing a single markdown table
   reception can work through row by row.
2. Anything the story leaves genuinely undecided must be visible in the
   document as an open question rather than settled silently on your way to
   writing a row.
3. Out of scope: automated tests, the back-office override screen, and the SMS
   provider integration.
evals.expected_output:
1. Produce `docs/test-cases/BOOK-77.md` containing a single markdown table
   reception can work through row by row.
2. Anything the story leaves genuinely undecided must be visible in the
   document as an open question rather than settled silently on your way to
   writing a row.
3. Out of scope: automated tests, the back-office override screen, and the SMS
   provider integration.
assertions: docs/test-cases/BOOK-77.md exists and contains a markdown table with rows. Scores zero if the output is prose only or written elsewhere.

For each of the three limits - 2-hour lead time, 90-day horizon, 3 upcoming appointments - the table contains a case at the last permitted value and a case at the first refused value (for example: a slot exactly 2 hours away and one 1 minute inside that; day 90 and day 91; a patient holding 2 then 3 then a 4th attempt). Scores zero if two or more of the three limits are covered on one side only, or with a value far from the limit ('a slot next week', 'a date next year'). Scores at most half if exactly one limit is one-sided.

The document states, as an open question or flagged assumption, that the story does not say whether exactly 2 hours ahead is bookable and whether cancellation exactly 24 hours before is free. Scores zero if one interpretation is written into the expected results with nothing marking it as a choice the story did not make. Raising only one of the two scores at most half.

At least one row targets the conversion between the stored UTC instant and the clinic's local rendering - a slot on the night the clocks change, or a lead-time / horizon calculation spanning the transition. Scores zero if timezone never appears in any precondition or expected value; the implementation note is the only place this is stated, so omitting it means the note was not read as test input.

At least one row makes the 3-appointment cap turn on what counts toward it - a cancelled appointment, or one whose start time has passed but which is not yet closed. Scores zero if every cap row assumes three plain future bookings.

The table must not contain three or more rows that differ only by slot duration (15 / 30 / 60) or by which arbitrary future slot was chosen, while asserting the same outcome. Duration only earns separate rows where the expected result differs. Three or more such interchangeable rows score zero here.

Each row carries a classification drawn from a small fixed vocabulary that separates a short confidence pass from fuller coverage and from edge and rejection work - for example smoke / regression / edge / negative. Scores zero if there is no classification column. An ad-hoc column with per-row free text and no consistent vocabulary scores at most half.
Rows for refused bookings state both what the patient is told and that no appointment was created and no SMS was sent. Scores zero if refusal rows expect only 'an error is shown'.

evals.prompt:
# Checkout incidents all happen between page load and payment

## Problem Description

CHK-660 replaces the multi-step checkout with a single "Pay now" action on the
cart page. The tech design has been pasted into the story.

Our last three incidents on the current checkout have one thing in common:
none of them was in the payment code, and none of them reproduced when a tester
walked the flow start to finish in one go. In each case something about the
order was true when the page rendered and no longer true when the money moved.
The existing test list covers declined cards, expired cards and wrong CVV very
thoroughly, and covered none of the three.

We want the case list before this is built, and we want it to be usable in a
year: the tech design in the story will not survive contact with the sprint,
and the last list we wrote had to be rewritten when the endpoints were renamed.

## Output Specification

1. Produce `docs/test-cases/CHK-660.md` containing a single markdown table for
   the manual pass.
2. Each row must state the state the system has to be in before the action, and
   what a tester can observe afterwards.
3. Out of scope: automated tests, load testing, and the payment provider's own
   3-D Secure screens.
evals.expected_output:
1. Produce `docs/test-cases/CHK-660.md` containing a single markdown table for
   the manual pass.
2. Each row must state the state the system has to be in before the action, and
   what a tester can observe afterwards.
3. Out of scope: automated tests, load testing, and the payment provider's own
   3-D Secure screens.
assertions: docs/test-cases/CHK-660.md exists and contains a markdown table with rows. Scores zero if prose only or written elsewhere.

At least three rows put a change between the precondition and the action rather than inside it: the last unit of a line sold to someone else, a price or delivery cost changing, the session token expiring during the 30 minutes on the page, the cart edited in another tab, the saved card removed or expiring in the meantime. Scores zero if every row assumes the cart, stock, prices and session observed at page load still hold at submit. One or two such rows score at most half.

At least one row covers the provider confirming the charge while the order is not durably created - the 20-second timeout elapsing with the outcome unknown, or the promotion failing after the charge. Its expected result must state what the shopper is charged and what a support agent can observe, not merely 'an error page is shown'. Scores zero if the only failure rows are the provider declining. A row that names the timeout but expects only an error message scores at most half.

A row covers the action being submitted twice - double press, browser back then re-submit, or a retry after a timeout - and pins that exactly one charge and one order exist afterwards. Scores zero if repeat submission never appears. Asserting only that a second confirmation page is shown, without pinning the charge count, scores at most half.

Steps and expected results must describe behaviour, not internals. Any row naming PayNowButton, POST /v3/checkout/confirm, PaymentIntent, or orders_staging in its steps or expected result is implementation-coupled and churns with the first refactor. Three or more such rows score zero here; one or two score at most half. Naming an internal only in a precondition that has no behavioural equivalent is not penalised.

Where the story does not define what should happen - stock disappearing mid-flow, the timeout, a partial write - the row says the behaviour is not specified and states the proposed contract as a proposal, rather than inventing an expected result and presenting it as required. Scores zero if every such row asserts an outcome the story never gives with nothing marking it.

Preconditions specify the state that matters - stock level on the line, saved card present, session age, cart contents - by fixture or by value. Scores zero if preconditions are uniformly 'logged-in user with items in cart'.

Expected results across the table include stock decremented, order created with the charged amount, and the confirmation email, not only what the shopper sees. Scores zero if every expected value is a screen observation.

evals.prompt:
# Evidence upload spec is mostly a list of file formats

## Problem Description

CLM-512 lets a policyholder attach evidence to a claim. The spec is short and
most of it is the list of accepted formats, so the test list we got back last
time was six rows long: one per format, each saying the file uploads.

That list ran green for two releases while a renamed executable sailed through
the type check, a 0-byte file created an attachment row with nothing behind it,
and the eleventh file on a claim replaced the first instead of being refused.

The claims team runs a short confidence pass on this screen at every release
and a fuller pass weekly, and they need to know which rows belong to which.
They will not review more than about sixteen rows, so the budget is real:
anything that does not buy coverage is taking the place of something that
would.

## Output Specification

1. Produce `docs/test-cases/CLM-512.md` containing a single markdown table.
2. Keep it to roughly sixteen rows. A reviewer must be able to tell which rows
   are for the per-release confidence pass and which are not.
3. Out of scope: automated tests, the virus-scanner vendor's own behaviour, and
   the claims adjuster's review screen.
evals.expected_output:
1. Produce `docs/test-cases/CLM-512.md` containing a single markdown table.
2. Keep it to roughly sixteen rows. A reviewer must be able to tell which rows
   are for the per-release confidence pass and which are not.
3. Out of scope: automated tests, the virus-scanner vendor's own behaviour, and
   the claims adjuster's review screen.
assertions: docs/test-cases/CLM-512.md exists and contains a markdown table with rows. Scores zero if prose only or written elsewhere.

Accepted formats are collapsed into one or two rows - a single representative, or one parameterised row naming the set - and the freed rows go to classes with different outcomes. To score full marks at least six of these must appear: rejected format, contents disagreeing with the extension, 0-byte file, file at exactly 25 MB, file above 25 MB, tenth vs eleventh attachment, connection dropped mid-upload, scan-pending state, scan-failed state, claim not in state `open`, name at or over 200 characters, non-ASCII or emoji file name. Fewer than three scores zero. Three to five scores at most half.

Four or more rows that differ only by which accepted format was uploaded while asserting the same outcome score zero on this criterion. HEIC may earn its own row because the story gives it a different client path; the other five do not.

A row uploads a file whose real content does not match its extension or declared type - an executable or archive renamed to .pdf, a text file named .xlsx - and pins that it is refused rather than stored. Scores zero if the table only ever varies the extension. This is one of the three named production defects.

Rows exist for a file at exactly 25 MB and for one just above it, plus a 0-byte file. Scores zero if the only size row is 'a very large file is rejected'. Scores at most half if the cap is covered on one side only or the 0-byte case is missing.

A row adds the tenth attachment successfully and another attempts an eleventh, pinning that the existing ten are unchanged. Scores zero if the cap appears only as 'cannot exceed the limit' with no count in the precondition.

Each row carries a classification from a small fixed vocabulary separating the per-release confidence pass from fuller coverage, edge work and rejection work - for example smoke / regression / edge / negative. Scores zero if there is no classification column. Free-text per-row priority with no consistent vocabulary scores at most half.
Rows carry identifiers including the story key, in a form like CLM-512-TC-04. Scores zero with no identifier column; bare sequence numbers with no story key score at most half.

evals.prompt:
# Weekly digest story is going into the sprint on Monday

## Problem Description

NOTIF-31 is on the board for sprint planning on Monday. It came from a customer
call, was written up in about five minutes, and has not been through refinement.

The last time we took a notification story in at this quality, the team built
it, QA signed off against the acceptance criteria as written, and we found out
in production that the digest was going to every account in the database
including trial accounts that had never logged in, and that a customer who had
unsubscribed from marketing email was still getting it. Both were defensible
readings of the story. Neither had been asked about.

Engineering wants the case list up front, and the delivery lead wants to know
before Monday whether this story can be estimated as written or whether it
needs to go back for a refinement pass first.

## Output Specification

1. Produce `docs/test-cases/NOTIF-31.md`. It must serve both readers: the
   tester who will eventually execute against it, and the delivery lead who has
   to make the Monday call.
2. Anything in the document that rests on a reading of the story rather than on
   the story itself must be visibly identifiable as such by someone skimming.
3. Out of scope: automated tests, the email template's HTML, and the
   deliverability of our sending domain.
evals.expected_output:
1. Produce `docs/test-cases/NOTIF-31.md`. It must serve both readers: the
   tester who will eventually execute against it, and the delivery lead who has
   to make the Monday call.
2. Anything in the document that rests on a reading of the story rather than on
   the story itself must be visibly identifiable as such by someone skimming.
3. Out of scope: automated tests, the email template's HTML, and the
   deliverability of our sending domain.
assertions: docs/test-cases/NOTIF-31.md exists and contains both a table of cases and identifiable prose. Scores zero if written elsewhere.

The document names, as blocking gaps, at least three of: who the recipients are (all members / active members / opted-in members / trial accounts), whose timezone 08:00 refers to, what the observable result of a send is beyond the email arriving (a record, a suppression, a next-send timestamp), what happens when the 7-day window contains no activity, and how unsubscribe interacts with a digest that is arguably transactional. Scores zero if the document proceeds to a full case list without naming any gap. Naming gaps only as a general remark such as 'some details need clarification', without saying which fields, scores at most half.

No row may put a decision the story never made into its expected result as settled fact - recipient set, timezone, no-activity behaviour, or unsubscribe precedence. Two or more such rows score zero here. Rows that state the same content but are explicitly flagged as resting on an assumption do not count against this criterion.

Rows that can only be executed once a gap is closed carry a visible marker linking them to that specific open question, so re-work after refinement is bounded. Scores zero if provisional and settled rows are indistinguishable. A single blanket disclaimer at the top of the document, with nothing per row, scores at most half.

The document raises that 'Monday at 08:00' is undefined across timezones for a 400-person workspace and that the story does not say whether the send is per-workspace or per-recipient. Scores zero if a timezone interpretation is chosen and used without comment.
Cases or questions cover a workspace with nothing to report in the window, and a recipient who has unsubscribed or been deactivated between scheduling and sending. Scores zero if both are absent.

The document states plainly whether the story can be estimated as written or needs refinement first, with the gaps as the reason. Scores zero if the reader has to infer the answer from the presence of open questions.

The document is not only a list of questions: it contains executable cases for the parts the story does settle - the 7-day content categories, the links back into the workspace, the unsubscribe link's presence. Scores zero if no concrete cases are produced at all.

evals.prompt:
# Folder sharing: we only ever test it with a colleague who is sitting there

## Problem Description

SHARE-204 rebuilds the "share this folder" dialog. Every time we test sharing,
someone types the address of the person at the next desk, it works, and we
sign it off.

Two of our last four support escalations on the old dialog were about who the
address resolved to rather than about the sharing itself. One customer's
contractor had an account on a different workspace under the same email
address, and the share landed somewhere nobody could explain. Another shared to
a colleague who had been deactivated three weeks earlier and assumed it had
gone through.

The story below is what product wrote. It says a lot about what happens when
everything is in order and very little about anything else. We want the list of
what to check before we build it, not after.

## Output Specification

1. Produce `docs/test-cases/SHARE-204.md` containing a single markdown table
   for the manual pass.
2. Each row must be a situation worth checking on its own, at a size someone
   could pick up and execute — not an individual interaction with the dialog.
3. Out of scope: automated tests, the notification email template, and the
   billing consequences of adding a guest seat.
evals.expected_output:
1. Produce `docs/test-cases/SHARE-204.md` containing a single markdown table
   for the manual pass.
2. Each row must be a situation worth checking on its own, at a size someone
   could pick up and execute — not an individual interaction with the dialog.
3. Out of scope: automated tests, the notification email template, and the
   billing consequences of adding a guest seat.
assertions: docs/test-cases/SHARE-204.md exists and contains a markdown table with rows. Scores zero if prose only or written elsewhere.

Separate rows cover an address that matches no account, an address matching an account that exists but is deactivated or deleted, and an address matching an account that belongs to a different workspace or tenant than the folder. Scores zero if none of the three appears. Scores at most half if only one of the three appears. The cross-workspace row must pin that access is not granted to the foreign account rather than leaving the outcome as 'an error'.

At least one row changes the folder's state or the actor's standing between opening the dialog and confirming - folder moved to trash, folder ownership transferred, actor's own access revoked mid-flow. Scores zero if every row assumes the folder is present, owned by the actor, and unchanged throughout.

The table has a row per actor standing attempting the share - owner, editor, viewer - rather than only the owner. Because the story states editors and viewers are undecided, the non-owner rows must either state the expected refusal or be marked as blocked on the product decision. Scores zero if only the owner ever shares. Covering non-owners without noting the story leaves their behaviour open scores at most half.

A row shares with someone who already has access inherited from a parent folder, and pins whether the explicit grant raises, lowers, or is refused. Scores zero if inheritance never appears; it is stated in the notes and is the classic source of silently downgraded access.

A row shares with an address outside the workspace's verified domains while the admin restriction is on, and one covers the restriction being off. Scores zero if the restriction is never a precondition anywhere.

Each refusal row's expected result includes the negative postcondition - the target does not appear in the people list and cannot open the folder - not only what the sharer sees on screen. Scores zero if every refusal row asserts only a message.

Rows must be scenarios, not steps. A row whose whole content is one interaction with the dialog - 'opens the share dialog', 'types an email address', 'selects editor from the dropdown' - is a procedure step, not a case. Two or more such rows score zero here.

evals.prompt:
# Invoice rendering is only ever checked in English and dollars

## Problem Description

BILL-905 rebuilds the customer invoice: the PDF attachment and the email that
carries it. We are shipping it to the whole customer base, which after last
year's expansion is roughly 40% outside the United States.

The current invoice test list is nine rows and every one of them uses the same
seeded customer: a US company, USD, English. It has been green throughout two
separate billing complaints — one where a Japanese customer's totals came out
with two decimal places that do not exist in their currency, and one where a
German customer's invoice showed an amount that read as a thousand times too
small to their finance team.

The story and the finance note are below. Finance will review the list, so an
expected result has to be something they can look at an invoice and check, not
a judgement call.

## Output Specification

1. Produce `docs/test-cases/BILL-905.md` containing a single markdown table.
2. Out of scope: automated tests, the tax engine's own rate tables, and the PDF
   library's performance.
evals.expected_output:
1. Produce `docs/test-cases/BILL-905.md` containing a single markdown table.
2. Out of scope: automated tests, the tax engine's own rate tables, and the PDF
   library's performance.
assertions: docs/test-cases/BILL-905.md exists and contains a markdown table with rows. Scores zero if prose only or written elsewhere.

Rows cover at least a currency with no minor unit (JPY), a locale whose decimal separator is a comma and whose symbol trails (German EUR), and a right-to-left interface language, and each states the exact form the invoice must show - for example a whole-yen total with no decimal part, and 1.234,56 followed by the euro symbol. Scores zero if every row uses one currency and one language. Scores at most half if other locales appear but the expected result is 'renders correctly', 'is localised', or 'formatting is right for the locale'.

Rows that differ only by which language or currency was selected while asserting the same generic outcome add no coverage. Three or more such interchangeable rows score zero here. A locale earns its own row when the rule it exercises differs - minor units, separator, direction, script.

Rows distinguish domestic rate, EU cross-border reverse charge with a valid VAT number (0.00 tax plus the statement plus both numbers), a business without a VAT number, and 0% versus exempt printing different labels. Scores zero if reverse charge is absent. Treating 0% and exempt as one case scores at most half.

At least one row puts a non-Latin or long customer-supplied billing name and address on an invoice whose interface language is different - a Japanese company name on an English invoice, a German address block against a fixed-width label - and pins that the characters render rather than dropping to boxes or truncating silently. Scores zero if the customer name is Latin ASCII in every row.

A row pins the invoice date format so that a date such as 03/04/2026 cannot be read two ways, and a row pins the net-14 due date across a month or year boundary and states which entity's or customer's day is being counted. Scores zero if dates never appear as an expected value.

At least two rows cover paths that are not a clean invoice - an invalid or unverifiable VAT number, a zero-amount or credit invoice, a missing billing address, a customer whose currency and legal entity combination is not supported. Scores zero if every row produces a normal invoice.
Rows carry an identifier including the story key and name the acceptance criterion or finance-note rule they come from. Scores zero if neither is present; one of the two scores at most half.

evals.prompt:
# The onboarding test list is just the click-through with a table around it

## Problem Description

ONB-23 rebuilds the new-workspace onboarding wizard. What the backlog carries
is a short story plus the click-through support wrote for their own use, which
is a numbered walkthrough of the current wizard.

We asked a contractor for a test list last time and got twelve rows back: step
one became row one, step two became row two, and so on to the end. Running all
twelve in order is the same as running the walkthrough once — if the wizard is
reachable at all they all pass together, and if it is not they all fail
together, so the list tells us nothing we did not already know from the first
row. Meanwhile nobody has ever tested what happens when someone abandons the
wizard halfway and comes back the next day, which is the most common thing our
users actually do.

The team runs a short confidence pass on onboarding at every release and a
fuller pass weekly, so the list has to say which rows belong where.

The walkthrough also refers to the current build's internals. The wizard is
being rebuilt, so anything tied to those will not survive the sprint.

## Output Specification

1. Produce `docs/test-cases/ONB-23.md` containing a single markdown table.
2. Every row must be worth running on its own: it must be able to fail while
   its neighbours pass, and it must tell the reader something specific when it
   does.
3. Out of scope: automated tests, the marketing site that links into the wizard,
   and the pricing of the plans themselves.
evals.expected_output:
1. Produce `docs/test-cases/ONB-23.md` containing a single markdown table.
2. Every row must be worth running on its own: it must be able to fail while
   its neighbours pass, and it must tell the reader something specific when it
   does.
3. Out of scope: automated tests, the marketing site that links into the wizard,
   and the pricing of the plans themselves.
assertions: docs/test-cases/ONB-23.md exists and contains a markdown table with rows. Scores zero if prose only or written elsewhere.

Rows must be independently meaningful scenarios, not the walkthrough's steps re-tabulated. A row whose whole content is one interaction with one control - entering the name, pressing Continue, selecting a plan, confirming a component renders - is a procedure step. Scores zero if half or more of the rows correspond one-to-one with the numbered walkthrough steps, or if the table walks the four wizard steps in order as its organising principle. Scores at most half if three or more single-interaction rows remain.

Rows cover leaving the wizard partway and returning - signing in again and resuming at the first incomplete step, refreshing mid-step, navigating back to a completed step and changing an answer. Scores zero if every row runs the wizard start to finish in one sitting, which is the named gap. One such row scores at most half.

Steps and expected results must describe behaviour. Any row naming #company-name, PlanPicker, or POST /v2/onboarding/complete inherits the walkthrough's coupling to a build that is being replaced. Two or more such rows score zero here; one scores at most half.

Rows exercise the workspace-name rules at their edges (1, 2, 40 and 41 characters, and a name already used on the account) and the invite step by count (none, one, 25, 26) rather than by a single 'invites some teammates' row. Scores zero if neither limit is exercised at its edge. Covering one of the two scores at most half.

Rows cover skipping both optional steps, skipping one and not the other, and arriving with a plan pre-selected by the query parameter. Scores zero if the wizard is only ever completed on the same path the walkthrough takes.

Each row carries a classification from a small fixed vocabulary separating the per-release confidence pass from fuller coverage, edge work and rejection work - for example smoke / regression / edge / negative. Scores zero if there is no classification column; free-text per-row priorities with no consistent vocabulary score at most half.

Rows carry an identifier including the story key and an expected result a tester can observe. Scores zero if rows have no identifier, or if expected results are predominantly 'the step completes' / 'it works'.

evals.expected_output:
1. Produce `docs/test-cases/PAY-318.md` containing a single markdown table our

# Nobody can tell which search cases to re-run when an AC changes

## Problem Description

SRCH-88 has been re-scoped twice. AC-4 was rewritten in both sprints, and both
times the same thing happened: the QA lead re-read all thirty-odd cases from
the previous list line by line, guessed which ones AC-4 touched, and re-ran a
superset to be safe. The second pass cost two days.

Product has told us AC-4 will probably move again once the pricing experiment
lands, and there is an open question on AC-6 that will change something.

So the list we build this time has to survive that. When any single line of
this story changes, the person holding it must be able to work out in one pass
over the document which rows are affected — without reading each row's steps
and reconstructing where they came from.

Note that not everything a tester needs is in the acceptance criteria. Some of
it is in the mockup caption, and some of it is not written down anywhere.

## Output Specification

1. Produce `docs/test-cases/SRCH-88.md` containing a single markdown table.
2. The document must support the re-run problem described above directly: a
   reviewer holding a changed line of the story should be able to identify the
   affected rows by reading the table, not by inference.
3. Out of scope: automated tests, the relevance ranking algorithm itself, and
   the analytics events the search box emits.

assertions: docs/test-cases/SRCH-88.md exists and contains a markdown table with rows. Scores zero if prose only or written elsewhere.

The table has a dedicated field on every row naming the exact origin of that row - AC-4, AC-6, 'Frame 4 caption', or a quoted story sentence. Scores zero if no such field exists, or if it exists on fewer than half the rows. Scores at most half if the field is present throughout but identifies only the section ('acceptance criteria', 'mockup') rather than which specific bullet or caption.

An origin field whose value is 'Story', 'AC', 'Spec', 'Requirements', or blank defeats the entire purpose - it cannot answer 'which rows does the AC-4 rewrite affect'. Three or more rows carrying a generic value score zero here; one or two score at most half.

Rows covering behaviour no line of the story states - a one-character query, punctuation or wildcard characters in the query, filters that exclude everything, back navigation restoring filter state, a shared URL opened in a fresh session - carry an origin that says so explicitly ('implied by AC-7, not stated', 'no AC covers this'). Scores zero if such rows are attributed to an unrelated AC bullet as though the bullet stated them, which is worse than a blank field because it misdirects the re-run. Scores zero as well if no implied rows exist at all.

The empty-results state - query echoed back, chips still active, clear-filters re-running the query - has at least one row whose origin names the Frame 4 caption rather than an AC bullet. Scores zero if the empty state is missing entirely; covering it but tracing it to an AC bullet that does not mention it scores at most half.

The document records that the tie-break behaviour for equally-scored results is undecided, and any row touching ordering is marked as blocked on that decision. Scores zero if a tie-break behaviour is asserted as expected output as though the story had decided it.

At least two rows cover paths that do not return a normal result page - query under the minimum length, no matches, page number beyond the last page. Scores zero if every row ends in results being shown.

Each row is a scenario a tester could pick up and run. Rows whose whole content is a single interaction ('types into the search box', 'clicks a filter chip') are procedure steps; two or more score zero here.
